parents.title: Prime squares shift the center for quadratic Dirichlet L-values

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: A component discarded as error in one family becomes a leading deterministic bias in another. Separating this bias from the fluctuating prime terms reveals that the transferable object is a centered prime polynomial, not the unmodified zeta expression.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: The prime-square sub-sum bridges local character identities to the global family center. Quadratic reciprocity and Pólya-Vinogradov replace time orthogonality when averaging the remaining character polynomial over discriminants.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: The span states the GRH-conditional majorant, identifies the coherent prime-square contribution as one half log log x because chi_d(p^2)=1 away from conductor divisors, and shifts the large-value threshold accordingly. It names quadratic reciprocity and Pólya-Vinogradov for the analogue of Lemma 3 and states moderate-tail, larger-tail, and k(k+1)/2 moment bounds.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: For quadratic Dirichlet L-values, the source states a GRH-conditional prime-power upper majorant analogous to the zeta proposition. Prime squares contribute asymptotically one half log log x because χ_d(p²)=1 for p not dividing d. After shifting the large-value threshold by one half log log X, quadratic reciprocity and the Pólya-Vinogradov inequality furnish the analogue of the mean-value argument, giving Gaussian-type moderate tails, V log V-type larger tails, and an upper moment bound of symplectic exponent k(k+1)/2 up to ε.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The argument is sketched rather than fully derived and is conditional on GRH. The tail and moment upper bounds do not prove the conjectural Gaussian law, and conductor divisibility exceptions must remain controlled. The positive half-log-log shift and named averaging tools are clear; exact thresholds, constants, and displayed exponents are formula-sensitive. Calling the square contribution a deterministic bias and the remainder a centered fluctuating prime polynomial accurately captures the non-paraphrase operation. The need to control conductor-divisibility exceptions follows from the explicit p not dividing d qualification. Exact shifts, signs, and exponents are formula-sensitive; the prose nevertheless secures their qualitative roles.

parents.title: Prime squares shift the center oppositely for elliptic-curve twists

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The transfer to quadratic twists of an elliptic curve is modular at the prime-power level: degrees at least three are absorbed into O(1), while the prime-square layer contributes a coherent negative half-log-log term. Accounting for that term shifts the large-value threshold before the earlier family tail argument is reused, and the resulting moment upper bound has exponent k(k−1)/2 (up to ε). Thus local Euler coefficients do more than decorate an existing estimate: their square contribution changes the deterministic center while leaving the residual fluctuation-control route recognizable. The gain is reuse of the prime-polynomial architecture after recentering; the loss is that the sketch supplies only conditional upper-tail and moment control, not a full limiting law or a complete family proof.

parents.title: Gaussian centers distinguish unitary, symplectic, and orthogonal families

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Standardizing log central L-values separates two roles that can otherwise be conflated: a family-dependent center and a logarithmic fluctuation scale. The conjectural comparison places unitary values at zero mean, quadratic-Dirichlet values at a positive center, and positive-sign elliptic-curve twists at a negative center, while retaining variance on a log-log scale. This common frame gains a way to compare fixed standardized upper deviations across the three families, but an upper normal-tail bound under GRH is not a Gaussian limit. The remaining proof burden is explicitly two-sided and spectral: a Selberg-type analogue additionally needs most family members to avoid zeros very near 1/2; positive-sign restriction is also essential for the elliptic-curve twists because the other sign forces the central value to vanish.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Builds a standardized comparison that separates center from fluctuation, then performs a logical gap analysis between a one-sided conditional tail bound and a full distribution theorem.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted after removing causal claims absent from this exact span and replacing the vague representation language with the stated upper-tail versus full-law distinction. accepted_interpretation.source_support: The span states Keating-Snaith conjectural Gaussian laws with zero, positive, and negative means for the unitary, symplectic, and positive-sign orthogonal cases, respectively, and gives their log-log variance scales. It says the paper's ideas yield, assuming GRH, an upper bound by a Gaussian tail for fixed standardized deviations, and that Selberg's techniques require the added hypothesis that most relevant L-functions have no zero very near 1/2. It explicitly explains the sign restriction by forced central vanishing.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The three conjectural laws, sign restriction, GRH-conditional upper bound, and added zero-avoidance requirement are source facts. The center/fluctuation separation and proof-gap analysis are interpretations; no prime-square or prime-level causal attribution is imported from preceding units.
